text: This is the customer. They want a 3D image rendered. They see the price up front, and they order it.
And this is where it runs. The reference house in Basel, on the fifteenth of January, eight in the morning, minus two degrees outside. It needs about nine kilowatts of heat.
There are eleven servers in the basement, and right now all eleven are on. It's cold and the tank has room, so every bit of their heat gets used.
Back out on the map, the same scheduler runs a hospital and a spa too. At minus two, everyone wants heat... so the image is cut into sixty parts, and every building renders a share.
Now say the family stops using heat, and the house's tank is full. Watch the part it's working on.
The rack stops halfway, saves exactly where it got to, and a building that still needs heat finishes it from there. Nothing gets computed twice.
Same buildings, the fifteenth of July, two in the afternoon. The house only needs hot water now, so just one of its eleven servers runs. The spa still heats its pool, so the work goes there.
And this isn't only on screen. It's the same scheduler code, controlling a real AI job on this laptop, as one server of the reference house on that July day.
No heat needed... the job pauses. Heat needed again... it carries on from exactly where it was.
